chunks: Ground plane pros and cons. The question: What is a ground plane? Pros/cons?
A ground plane is a continuous layer of copper tied to ground, usually right under the signal layers. It is the reference and the return path for everything above it.
Its big benefit is a return path with very low resistance and inductance that keeps current loops small.
Its costs are extra layers, unwanted capacitance on nearby sensitive points, and trouble if you cut slots in it.
Picture a wide, smooth floor in a big hall. Wherever you walk, you can come straight back, so your round trip stays short.
But a floor sits close to everything, so it also touches things you wanted to keep apart. A crack in the floor forces you to walk around it, which is a slot forcing a detour.
The analogy is loose: a fast return current flows directly under its trace, not wherever it likes.
The benefits all come from one property: a large, low-impedance conductor sits a small distance from the signals.
The same property causes the costs: it also sits close to everything else, so it adds capacitance, shares currents, and needs to stay unbroken.
Return path: the route current takes back to its source ("Which layers should be ground"). Plane vs pour: a plane is a nearly solid layer.
A pour is copper fill on a signal layer, broken up by traces. Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square patch of copper, any size, about 0. 48 milliohms for standard foil.
Parasitic capacitance: unwanted capacitance between a trace or pad and the plane ("Parasitic elements on a PCB").
Slot or split: a gap in the plane that makes the return current detour.
For the benefit, compare resistances. A 0. 25 mm wide, 100 mm long trace is 400 squares, so about 400 times 0. 48 = 192 milliohms.
A plane over the same distance is about 1 square, so about 0. 48 milliohms. For the cost, a 1 mm² pad 0. 2 mm above the plane adds about 0. 19 picofarads.
On a sensitive amplifier input with a 1 megohms resistor, it is enough to slow the circuit and make it ring. So you cut the plane away under that one spot. That is the whole idea.
"A ground plane is a solid copper layer used as the reference and return path.
Pros: very low impedance, tiny return loops so less radiation, pickup and crosstalk, controlled-impedance traces, shielding between layers, heat spreading, and capacitance with a nearby power plane.

Cons: extra layers and cost, parasitic capacitance on high-impedance or RF nodes, shared-impedance noise if big currents flow through it, damage if you cut it, possible plane resonance, and thermal issues when soldering."
